Paradise has two gardens of silver and two of gold, a hollow-pearl pavilion sixty miles wide, and a tree whose shade a rider cannot cross in a hundred years.
Ibn Abbas says Surat al-Hashr, or Surat an-Nadir, concerned Bani an-Nadir, and a verse says the Prophet's burning and cutting down of their palm trees was by Allah's leave.
Bani an-Nadir's properties came to the Prophet without a Muslim expedition and were his alone; he took his wives' yearly expenses from them, the rest going to arms and horses.
Ibn Mas'ud curses women who tattoo, pluck facial hair or space their teeth, as the Prophet did, citing verse 59.7, and the Prophet cursed women using false hair.
Umar urges his successor to be kind to the Ansar, and an Ansari couple give the Prophet's guest their children's food, prompting a verse on preferring others.
Hatib's letter to Meccan pagans is intercepted; the Prophet accepts his reason and spares him as one of Badr, and verse 60.1 on befriending enemies is said to concern him.
The Prophet takes the pledge of believing women by word alone, never touching their hands, against worshipping others, stealing, adultery and wailing for the dead, and men pledge likewise.
The Prophet names himself Muhammad, Ahmad, Al-Mahi through whom disbelief is wiped out, Al-Hashir at whose feet people are gathered, and Al-Aqib.
Asked who the others in verse 62.3 are, the Prophet puts his hand on Salman and says men of his people would reach faith even at the Pleiades.
A caravan arrived on a Friday and all but twelve left the Prophet for it, and the verse on people dispersing headlong to a bargain was revealed.
Zaid bin Arqam reports Abdullah bin Ubai's words, is disbelieved when Ibn Ubai swears denial, until Surat al-Munafiqun confirms him; the Prophet refuses to let Umar kill Ibn Ubai.
Ibn Umar divorced his wife during her menses; the Prophet, angry, ordered him to take her back and divorce, if he wished, only when she is clean and untouched.
A pregnant widow's waiting period ends when she delivers: Um Salama reports Subai'a gave birth forty days after her husband was killed and the Prophet married her off.
Ibn Abbas says a man who tells his wife 'You are unlawful to me' must make expiation, the Prophet being the example to follow.
Aisha and Hafsa plot over the honey the Prophet drank at Zainab's; Umar names them the two wives who backed each other and recounts the Prophet's seclusion and plain life.
Ibn Abbas says verse 68.13 was revealed about a man of Quraysh marked by a sign like the one hung on a sheep's neck.
The people of Paradise are the weak and humble whose oaths Allah fulfils, and the people of Hell are the violent, arrogant and stubborn.
Allah will lay bare His Shin and all believers will prostrate, but those who prostrated in the world to be seen will find their backs too stiff to bend.
Idols named after pious men of Noah's people, set up at Satan's prompting and worshipped once their origin was forgotten, were later worshipped by Arabs: Wadd, Suwa', Yaghouth, Ya'uq, Nasr.
Barred from heaven's news by flames, devils search the world and some hear the Prophet reciting at the Fajr prayer, believe, tell their people, and Surat al-Jinn is revealed.
Asked about the first surah, Jabir tells how the Prophet, frightened by the angel of Hira on a chair between sky and earth, asked to be wrapped, and Al-Muddaththir came.
The Prophet moved his tongue hurrying to memorise revelation, so verse 75.16 told him not to, Allah promising to collect and explain it, and he listened until Gabriel left.
Surat al-Mursalat was revealed to the Prophet in a cave as a snake escaped them, and Ibn Abbas explains its sparks like Al-Qasr by the logs they stored.
Forty separate the two trumpet blasts; then Allah sends rain, bodies grow like plants, and each is rebuilt from the coccyx, the one bone that does not decay.
Pointing with his index and middle fingers, the Prophet says his advent and the Hour are like these two fingers.
One who recites the Quran and knows it by heart will be with the noble scribes, and one who learns it with great difficulty gets a double reward.
Some will stand in sweat up to their ears before the Lord of the Worlds, and anyone whose account is questioned is ruined, the easy reckoning being only its presentation.
Ibn Abbas says 'from stage to stage' in the verse means from one state to another, and concerns the Prophet.
Al-Bara lists the first emigrants to reach Medina, who taught the Quran there, then Umar with twenty men, and the city's joy at the Prophet's arrival.
In a sermon the Prophet explains 91.12 on the man who hamstrung the she-camel, warns against lashing one's wife like a slave, and against laughing at breaking wind.
Abu Ad-Darda' confirms Alqama's reading 'By the male and the female', as heard from Ibn Mas'ud and from the Prophet, refusing the reading others want.
Everyone's place in Paradise or Hell is written, yet each should keep doing good, finding easy what leads there, the Prophet says, reciting verses on the path of ease.
Everyone's place in Paradise or the Fire is written, yet the Prophet tells his companions to keep doing deeds, as each finds easy what leads to his destined place.
When the ill Prophet missed his night prayer and Abu Lahab's wife said his Satan had forsaken him, Allah revealed that his Lord had neither forsaken nor hated him.
On a journey the Prophet recited Surat at-Tin in one of the first two rak'at of the Isha prayer.
Revelation began with true dreams and the angel in Hira telling the Prophet to read; Khadijah comforted him, Waraqa recognised the angel, and after a pause 'Arise and warn' came.
Abu Jahl threatens to tread on the Prophet's neck if he sees him praying at the Ka'bah, and the Prophet says the angels would snatch him away.
Allah orders the Prophet to recite Surah 98 to Ubai bin Ka'b, and Ubai weeps on learning that Allah mentioned him by name.
A horse brings reward, protection or sin according to why it is kept; for donkeys the Prophet cites the verse that every atom's weight of good or evil is seen.
Al-Kauthar is a river the Prophet saw when taken up to the heavens, with banks of hollow-pearl tents and countless vessels; Ibn Abbas calls it the good Allah gave him.
